The reaction, \(\mathrm{3\,ClO^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_3^{\ominus} + 2\,Cl^{\ominus}}\) occurs in two steps,

(i) \(\mathrm{2\,ClO^{-} \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus}}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{ClO_2^{\ominus} + ClO^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_3^{\ominus} + Cl^{\ominus}}\)

The reaction intermediate is
solution: [Textbook misprint: step (i) is printed as \(\mathrm{2\,ClO^{-} \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus}}\), which is not balanced — two chlorine atoms enter and one leaves. The step intended is \(\mathrm{2\,ClO^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus} + Cl^{\ominus}}\), which balances and which, added to step (ii), reproduces the overall equation given. The answer is unaffected: \(\mathrm{ClO_2^{\ominus}}\) is the species formed in step (i) and consumed in step (ii) under either reading.]

stem: Rate law for the reaction, \(\mathrm{2\,NO + Cl_2 \longrightarrow 2\,NOCl}\) is rate \(= k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2[\mathrm{Cl_2}]\). Thus \(k\) would increase with

options.label: D
options.text: increase of concentrations of both \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{NO}\)

solution: [Textbook misprint: the rate law is printed as rate \(= k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2[\mathrm{Cl_2}]\), but the reaction given contains no \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) at all; the intended concentration term is \([\mathrm{NO}]^2\). The answer is unaffected, since the question asks what \(k\) depends on and no concentration term appears in \(k\).]
